The Ayyubid Dynasty. From 1169 to 1260 of the common era, this was a Kurdish military clan founded by Saladin, who unified Egypt and the Levant and became Islam's most celebrated warrior-hero by defeating the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin. Though Saladin's successors could not maintain his unified empire, the Ayyubids established lasting Islamic governance in Egypt and inspired centuries of Islamic historical memory.

The Ayyubids were founded by Ayyub ibn Shadi, a Kurdish military officer. His son Saladin rose to power, serving as vizier to the Fatimid caliph before seizing control in 1171. Saladin, who ruled from 1169 to 1193, is the dynasty's defining figure—a commander who united fractious Islamic emirates, crushed the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, and recaptured Jerusalem. He became a legendary symbol of Islamic chivalry and resistance. The Ayyubids ruled Egypt, Syria, Palestine, Yemen, and parts of Mesopotamia, creating a vast unified realm that restored Sunni Islam and ended Shiite Fatimid rule. Saladin practiced relative magnanimity toward defeated enemies and religious minorities. After reconquering Jerusalem, he permitted Christian inhabitants safe passage rather than ordering a massacre, earning respect across Christendom. But Saladin's heirs fragmented the empire almost immediately after his death. His nephew Al-Adil and subsequent sons divided territories among themselves. By 1250 they were replaced by the Mamluk Sultanate, a slave-soldier military regime in Egypt, though Ayyubid princes lingered as nominal rulers in Syria until 1260.

The Fatimid Caliphate was the Shiite dynasty Saladin overthrew to establish Sunni rule. The Mamluk Sultanate eventually superseded their authority in Egypt. The Battle of Hattin was the 1187 victory that turned the tide of the Crusades. And Mecca was one of the holy cities that figured in their realm.
